title: Exploring nonlinear body oscillations for natural quadruped gaits - Nature Machine Intelligence
byline: Schmidt; Annika; Calzolari; Davide; Sachtler; Arne; Loeffl; Florian Christoph; Seidel; Daniel; Hermann; Milan; Burger; Robert; Gumpert; Thomas; Raffin; Antonin;
html:
Abstract

Animals’ body morphology shapes the gait patterns they can perform, where mechanical resonance reduces the need for active control. By tuning posture and muscle stiffness, they leverage their embodied intelligence to achieve effective gaits for different speeds. By contrast, most quadruped robots are not specifically designed to exploit mechanical resonance owing to the complexity of nonlinear dynamics and require dedicated locomotion controllers. To provide an alternative, we present a proof-of-concept framework making the nonlinear dynamics of a robot predictable in the design process and show how this knowledge can be leveraged such that multi-gait locomotion can emerge from nonlinear resonances—shaped by gravity, inertia and elasticity. Here we present the highly compliant quadruped robot eBert, on which we identify six nonlinear normal modes using our new theoretical tools and validate their existence in simulation and hardware. With black-box optimization to determine step length, simulations show how each nonlinear normal mode naturally develops into a distinct gait, manifesting different speeds, which also largely transfers to the robotic hardware. Our experiments show that eBert can exploit its mechanics to generate task-specific movements, which may serve as foundation for designing a new generation of agile and efficient robots leveraging embodied intelligence.

Main

Quadrupedal robots hold great potential for real-world applications owing to their inherent stability and weight-bearing capabilities, leading to a rapidly expanding market1,2. Despite improving capabilities, most quadrupeds converge on similar designs driven by stiff actuation with high-gain feedback, yielding gaits dictated by the controller rather than mechanics3. By contrast, animals achieve efficient, habitat-specific movement4 through tight coupling between morphology and neural wiring5,6. This integration enables locomotion to emerge from the natural interplay of mechanics and control7—a principle known as ‘embodied intelligence’8. One key aspect is that an animal’s morphology not only supports locomotion but also constrains and shapes its dynamics. Thus, an animal’s body structure determines which gaits it can perform9 and which are preferred at different speeds10,11. Hoyt and Taylor famously demonstrated this in horses, showing that switching gaits at specific speeds minimized energy costs12. To maintain energy efficiency across speeds, animals adjust their posture, gait patterns and muscle stiffness, effectively tuning their body’s resonance13,14, while the elasticity in tendons and muscles enhances robustness by absorbing impact energy15.

Motivated by these biomechanical insights, a line of research on legged locomotion has focused on including elastic elements in robotic designs16,17,18,19 and leveraging the added compliance through matched control strategies20,21,22,23. This extends early work on passive dynamic walkers that exploit intrinsic mechanical responses to generate inherently stable, energy-efficient locomotion, with dynamics well approximated by an inverted pendulum24. Adding a spring to the simple walking template resulted in the spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) model25,26,27, enabling the characterization of multiple gaits and their transitions. Several robotic experiments validated that exploiting elasticity increases energy efficiency and robustness18,28,29,30. Simulations of an elastic sagittal quadruped with prismatic legs showed that minimizing energy consumption with optimal control naturally produces different gaits at varying speeds31,32, consistent with biological observations. Adaptive oscillators, similar to the biological principle of central pattern generators (CPGs), proved effective to extract and excite the intrinsic frequencies of robotic hardware33,34. Notable examples include the works of Badri-Spröwitz and Ijspeert, demonstrating that locomoting robots inspired by biological mechanics can display natural gaits with remarkably simple CPG controllers18,29,33. Well-designed systems such as BirdBot can exhibit gaits even under open-loop control18, but feedback remains generally essential to entrain control frequency to intrinsic system dynamics and exploit compliance, as demonstrated on the quadruped Morti29. However, without explicit engineering, compliant hardware typically converges to a single gait pattern dictated by its dominant mechanical resonance.

Achieving different gaits through hardware properties requires meticulous design derived from detailed analysis of biological principles, as exemplified by the synergies implemented in the quadruped robot PAWS30. More generally, designing legged robots where the compliance enables multiple gaits remains a challenge3 because its typically nonlinear dynamics are difficult to predict in advance.

Recent advances in nonlinear mode theory enabled us to address this challenge and design hardware with diverse purposeful dynamics. Using mathematical tools based on differential geometry and algebraic topology35,36, we can analyse nonlinear oscillations in complex systems37 to identify families of periodic orbits in energy-conservative systems, including nonlinear normal modes (NNMs)38, which generalize linear eigenmodes to nonlinear dynamics. This offers a framework to systematically compute the natural dynamics even in complex, high-dimensional systems with pronounced nonlinearities. Building on the biological insight that efficient locomotion is tightly connected to exploiting body resonance10,13, we hypothesize that common quadrupedal gaits—such as trotting, pacing and bounding—may naturally arise from NNMs in purposefully designed quadrupeds. While the theoretical foundation of the NNM analysis has been established in prior work35,37, this paper presents the application of the framework to a full 3D quadruped robot to develop locomotion. This includes (1) the design of the highly elastic quadruped ‘eBert’, (2) the analysis of eBert’s nonlinear modes uncovering the robot’s natural movement tendencies and (3) the excitation of these modes to generate gaits using only minimal control.

Starting from biological leg stiffness approximations, eBert’s design encodes functional oscillations through its mechanics (Fig. 1a). Using our developed methods35,37,38, we identify six NNMs of conservative dynamics, which we validate in simulations and hardware, excited by a deliberately simple feedback-based state-switching controller to compensate for friction. Extending this controller to lift the feet according to a pattern matching each mode enables distinct, and biologically plausible gaits to emerge naturally from the robot’s dynamics (Fig. 1b).

a, Inspired by the elasticity of biological tendons and muscles, the quadruped robot eBert features series elastic actuation with soft springs to implement this function mechanically. High compliance in the hardware design results in a system that naturally displays large-amplitude oscillations in different directions. b, Leveraging the biological concept of embodied intelligence, the natural oscillations encoded in the robotic hardware can be exploited following three key aspects: first, the mathematical description and analysis of the system motions; second, the excitation of nonlinear resonance; and finally, the generation of (loco)motion patterns, leading to gaits that resemble the ones known in animals as depicted in the gait diagram indicating the stance phases of the left and right front legs (LF, RF) and hind legs (LH, RH).

With our hypothesis successfully validated, eBert demonstrates that diverse gaits can naturally emerge from purposefully designed nonlinear resonances, manifesting embodied intelligence in robotic hardware. Rather than replicating animal locomotion in stride, speed or efficiency, we claim to show that eBert’s emerging gaits follow biological principles where body resonance naturally organizes multi-legged coordination without explicit scripting. Our framework can guide robotic co-design with intrinsic oscillations tailored to desired tasks, while improved dynamics analysis can deepen understanding of biological movement, advancing both robotic and biological knowledge.

Results

The highly elastic quadruped eBert

Animal gaits can be viewed as periodic oscillations that exploit resonance of the musculoskeletal system to minimize energy expenditure13,14. Similarly, compliant robots can improve efficiency by exciting their natural resonances with controllers entrained to the mechanics33,39, but usually only one or few gaits arise from the most prominent resonance18,29. A richer locomotion repertoire based on resonances requires a robot that mechanically encodes multiple useful high-amplitude body oscillations, which we realized with the highly compliant quadruped eBert with 12 degrees of freedom (DOF).

eBert was designed with lightweight elastic legs and large enough compliance to encode multiple functional body oscillations at frequencies and amplitudes suitable for gait generation (Fig. 2a,b). The precise leg stiffness of eBert was estimated assuming the body dimensions of a small dog weighing 4.5 kg using calculations for animal leg stiffness40. Adapting the initial stiffness estimation such that eBert could stand upright without active corrections led to a stiffness of 6.55 N m rad−1 in the ‘hip’ and ‘knee’ joints, and 13 N m rad−1 in the ‘shoulders’. Design and stiffness details are outlined in the ‘Design for purposeful oscillations in eBert’ section in the Methods. The hardware elasticity was implemented using serial elastic actuators (SEAs), with springs having the respective stiffness at each joint. This can mimic the energy storage of animals’ muscles and tendons, but, unlike biology, SEA stiffness cannot be adjusted and is joint-local instead of distributed throughout the body13. Nevertheless, SEAs provide a practical way to add mechanical compliance in robots41 (Fig. 1a). With the implemented compliance, eBert encodes large mechanical oscillations in various directions, yielding much higher system compliance than previous elastic quadrupeds exploiting embodied intelligence29,30.

Replicating embodiment in robotics also requires control that matches the system dynamics. While mechanics and neural control are tightly coupled in animal bodies, robotics allows separate analysis of each to aid better understanding of individual contributions. In eBert we focused on the mechanical aspects encoding oscillations through design, only applying minimalistic control. We first analysed the inherently nonlinear system dynamics of eBert enabled by our recently developed numerical methods35,37 to identify the system’s NNMs. These NNMs extend the concept of linear normal modes, which characterize periodic coordinated oscillations of a mechanical system around an equilibrium with a constant amplitude and phase. By contrast, NNMs vary with energy levels, changing shape and period on curved surfaces called Eigenmanifolds35 (Fig. 2c). Using our methods, the NNMs of the conservative model can be computed, which describe intrinsic oscillations purely from the robot’s mechanical properties, without control input. Computational details are outlined in the Supplementary Methods.

We hypothesized that distinct gaits can emerge from the different NNMs. As starting point, we analysed eBert’s natural motion tendencies around a symmetric standing position (shoulders neutral, hips and knees slightly flexed) (Fig. 2b) with the commanded motor positions θ0 for the three joints per leg being

Assuming fixed foot positions but free rotations yields a constrained system with n = 6 DOFs and six corresponding linear modes, from which at least six NNMs were expected on the basis of the Seifert conjecture35.

The six computed NNMs are displayed in Fig. 2, with the associated eigenvectors w and their characteristic oscillation frequency of the linearized system summarized on the left side of Fig. 3. As predicted by theory, NNM frequency and shape vary with energy as the system enters the nonlinear regime at larger deflections (Fig. 2d,f). Sorting the NNMs by frequency revealed that the slowest mode (M1) is a translation of the robot body along the y axis coupled with rolling (Fig. 2b,d). The second mode (M2) couples a pitching oscillation with a forward–backward motion along the x axis. The third mode (M3) manifests as rotation around the z axis, going vertically through the body’s centre of mass (COM). The fourth motion (M4) is a translational up-and-down motion along the z axis. The fifth (M5) and sixth modes (M6) are the pure pitch and roll motions, respectively, both oscillating at much higher frequencies (Fig. 3, bottom left). Especially the first two modes show large amplitudes for higher energy levels, while the remaining modes only display small displacements in Cartesian space owing to the higher oscillation frequencies (Fig. 2d). The phase plot of each NNM for the respective dominant motion direction (Fig. 2e) still verifies the expected nonlinearity for all modes except M6, which appears to adhere to the special case of a ‘strict mode’36,38, which in this case also resembles a linear mode (Fig. 2d), and orbits project to concentric ellipses in the phase plot (Fig. 2e). The Supplementary Methods present more detailed quantification of the modes’ nonlinearity.

Values are presented for the initial standing pose (left) and the configuration used for stepping forward (right), calculated for the conservative model, in simulation with friction and from the hardware of eBert.

In essence, we demonstrated that eBert’s design encodes multiple distinct NNMs with large enough amplitudes, which are expected to serve as foundations for different gaits.

Existence of modal oscillations on hardware

To prove the practical relevance of the NNMs to develop locomotion in robotic hardware, predicted dynamics computed from the conservative eBert model must be excitable and sustainable in the real system, which is not energy-conservative and constantly loses energy, for example, due to friction. Thus, while NNMs are theoretically optimally efficient, sustaining them in hardware requires a controller to compensate for energy losses. Therefore, we implemented a state-switching controller derived in previous works inspired by human control strategies42,43. The controller functions analogously to pushing a playground-swing when it naturally comes to a halt on either side, avoiding motor commands during the system’s motion flow, which would disturb the natural dynamics. Alternative approaches, such as feedback-modulated CPGs23,29 or even feedforward control given the known system frequencies, could also be used to excite the oscillations. However, prior work comparing the alternatives44 showed the state-switching controller excites dynamics effectively with minimal tuning, motivating this choice for initial validation.

The controller injects an empirically defined energy θz at the extreme points, where the robot’s oscillation naturally subsides and the combined spring deflection τz (ref. 42) is maximal. Crossing a threshold ϵτ near equilibrium armed the control trigger (Fig. 4a), waiting to inject energy when the next direction change was detected from the combined Cartesian body velocity \({\dot{x}}_{b}\).
